Case study · Concept design

Helping Patients Remember What Was Said In The Room

Carry is a patient-facing companion for cancer surveillance. It helps someone prepare for an oncology appointment, capture what was actually said, and come back to it months later. This is the early-stage design work that gave the concept a shape stakeholders could react to.

RoleUX designer — flows, interface, design system sheet PhaseConcept exploration, pre-PRD ideation OutputFive flow designs, one reference sheet, one working prototype

Contents

  1. Context
  2. The problem
  3. What this work was
  4. The shape of the product
  5. Nine constraints
  6. Preparing for the conversation
  7. Capturing what was said
  8. Reviewing it later
  9. The visual language
  10. How it was made
  11. Where it stands

Context

Carry is a patient-facing mobile companion for cancer surveillance. It supports patients in active surveillance after primary cancer treatment, helping them prepare for and capture conversations with their oncologist across recurring testing cycles. The primary use case anchors to Signatera, a blood test that looks for traces of tumour DNA after treatment has ended.

Surveillance is a particular kind of waiting. Treatment is over. The patient is not sick in the way they were, but they are not finished either. Every few months there is a blood draw, then a wait, then a fifteen-minute appointment where a doctor tells them what the number means. Then it starts again.

The product covers three moments in that cycle: preparing for the conversation with the oncologist, capturing what was said during or after, and reviewing past conversations. Everything else in the design follows from those three.

A calmer way to keep track of your care.Carry, welcome screen

The problem

The appointment is short and the stakes are high, and people forget what they meant to ask. That is the premise the whole product rests on, and it is stated plainly in the brief:

Patients consistently report forgetting what they meant to ask their doctor during high-stakes appointments.Project brief, conversation preparation

Three more assumptions sit underneath it, each written down as background rather than discovered in the room. Patients refine questions as they think about them — a question that starts as “what does this mean?” becomes “what does this result mean for the rest of my surveillance schedule?” Patients need to capture what was said afterwards, and the working assumption is that they record on their own phone and upload it. And the value compounds over time: someone in cycle eight may want to look back at cycle three to understand a pattern or remember a follow-up.

On evidence. These are the product team's stated premises, not findings from research I ran. There was no interview study, no survey, and no usability testing behind this phase. The one research-shaped input on the board is a single node in the process diagram — “pain points surfaced: patient research, clinical feedback, strategic priorities” — which is where research would enter, not evidence that it did.

I have left it that way rather than dressing assumptions up as insights. What this project can honestly show is design judgment under constraint, not validated user need.

The patient in the prototype is seeded, and named as such: Sarah, 52, treated fourteen months ago for stage III colorectal cancer, in cycle four of surveillance with Dr. Maya Patel. Every screen is populated with realistic surveillance content rather than placeholder text, because a calm tone is impossible to evaluate against Lorem ipsum.

What this work was

Concept exploration, sized to the decision it needed to support.

The goal was narrow and written down: produce design artifacts that allow stakeholders to evaluate the Carry concept and provide direction on product scope, feature priorities, and visual direction. The audience was product leadership, design leadership, clinical advisors and the commercial team. Success meant they could review the five core flows, react to the visual language, say which features felt right, and decide whether to commit to a more serious design phase.

What it is

  • Concept exploration of a patient-facing surveillance companion
  • Five core flow designs to demonstrate the product's shape
  • A design system reference sheet to communicate the visual vocabulary
  • Source material for stakeholder discussion and direction-setting

What it is not

  • A fully developed component library
  • A complete design system with maintained tokens, variables and instances

That second list was a deliberate choice, not a shortfall. The designs use containers, frames and groups rather than components and variables, which keeps them malleable and avoids pushing premature decisions into a production library other teams depend on. As the brief puts it, this lets the design move fast and respond to stakeholder feedback “without the friction of maintaining a structured component library that may not survive review.”

The shape of the product

Five phases, one hub, and a path a patient can actually walk.

Before any screen work, the flow. Carry has an entry sequence, a hub, and three task phases that map to the three moments. The dashboard is the only place a patient returns to; everything else is entered from there and exits back to it.

Two things in that diagram were decisions rather than descriptions. The dashboard is a hub, not a feed — it holds the next conversation, a horizontal timeline of the surveillance journey, recent conversations, and outstanding follow-ups, and nothing else. And capture and review are separate destinations even though they show the same data, for reasons that come up below.

Nine constraints

Anticipated friction, and the decisions that resolved each.

Most of the interesting work on this project was subtraction. A product that sits between a cancer patient and their oncologist has a lot of things it must not do, and naming those early is what made the rest of the design straightforward.

Three of those are worth expanding, because they shaped the interface more than anything else.

Carry never records, and never delivers a result

Recording consent law varies by state, and an app that starts a recording inside a doctor's office can put a patient on the wrong side of it. So recording moved out of the product entirely. The patient records on their own phone, the way they already would, and uploads the file afterwards. Carry receives and transcribes; it never initiates.

The second boundary is sharper. Delivering results is the oncologist's job. Carry helps a patient prepare for and capture the conversation about a result. It never shows the result itself. That single rule removes a whole category of liability and, more importantly, keeps the product from becoming the thing that tells someone their cancer is back.

The AI matches; it does not author

The most novel part of the product is also the most dangerous. After a recording is transcribed, Carry fills in the patient's prepared questions with what the doctor said. If that answer were a summary, a wrong one could send someone into the next three months acting on a sentence no one ever said.

So matched answers are direct excerpts from the transcript, never generated prose. They carry a “Matched from recording” badge, they are editable, and editing swaps the badge to “Edited”. They can be dismissed, with an undo. Nothing in the interface implies the match is authoritative.

Constrained AI to matching, not authoring. The AI surfaces, never interprets.Constraints and resolutions, item 3

A question is never truncated

Patients write these questions specifically to ask their oncologist. Showing two-thirds of one and an ellipsis defeats the point. So question rows wrap and grow downward instead of clipping — 56 points tall for a short question, taller for a long one, on every device width. It is a small rule that quietly constrains every list in the product.

Preparing for the conversation

The heart of the product's value, and the screen with the most structure.

The preparation screen holds three things: a checklist of what to bring, the patient's own questions, and a library of suggested questions grouped into four categories. Suggested questions are starting points, not prescriptions — tapping one claims it into “My questions”, and tapping it again gives it back. The toggle is bidirectional and holds its state, so nothing is a one-way door.

Prototype

Sign in, then prepare for a conversation

The full entry path, then the preparation screen. Add a suggested question and watch it claim itself; open the menu on one of your own questions to edit, reorder or delete it. Everything here is seeded data running against a simulated state machine.

9:41

Try it — tap a suggested question to add it to your list.

Questions grow, never clip. A long question wraps and the row expands. At 440pt the same question fits one line and the row returns to 56pt.

Editing is inline. The row becomes a text field with a check and a close, rather than pushing to a separate screen. It respects the patient's place in the list.

Claiming is reversible. Adding a suggested question changes its icon to a filled check; tapping again removes it. A snackbar offers undo.

Nothing is celebrated. No exclamation marks, no emoji, no encouragement. Confirmations read “Session saved”, not “Session saved successfully”.

Capturing what was said

The upload flow, the permission moment, and the AI matching pattern.

The patient has just done the hard part. The upload flow has to be close to frictionless: tap upload, grant file access once, pick the recording, wait. The permission dialog says what it needs and why without legal-sounding language, and it is explicit about what Carry cannot see — only audio files, never photos or documents.

Prototype

Upload a recording and watch it transcribe

The recording panel is a state machine: empty, selecting, uploading, transcribing, transcribed. Timings are the real ones from the specification — two seconds to upload, three to transcribe — because a progress state that resolves instantly tells you nothing about how the wait feels.

9:41

Try it — tap Upload recording to start the flow.

Permission is asked once, plainly. “Carry never sees photos, documents, or other files.” The dialog names the limit, not just the request.

The file picker is a bottom sheet. Familiar as an iOS pattern, but drawn in Carry's own vocabulary rather than handed off to the system picker.

Progress is honest. Two linear progress states with different labels, so the patient can tell uploading from transcribing.

When transcription finishes, the questions the patient prepared start filling in. Not all of them — three of six in the seeded scenario. The rest stay unchecked, waiting for the patient to answer them from memory or leave them open. That gap is deliberate: a system that claims to have caught everything is a system you stop checking.

Prototype

See how a question meets the transcript

Each matched answer is an excerpt from what the doctor actually said, badged and editable. Expand a question to see the excerpt it came from; two of the six have no confident match and stay open.

9:41

Try it — expand a question to see the excerpt behind it.

Excerpts, not summaries. The words in the answer are the words in the recording.

Editable by design. Correcting a match changes the badge to “Edited”, so the provenance of every answer stays visible.

Unmatched stays unmatched. Questions the system could not answer are left plainly unchecked rather than filled with a guess.

Reviewing it later

The same record, in a different mood.

Capture and review are the same data and two different tasks. During and just after an appointment the patient is doing things: checking questions off, typing notes, adding follow-ups. Months later they are reading. Carrying the capture interface into review would leave a page full of checkboxes inviting action on a conversation that finished a long time ago.

So review mode takes the affordances away. No checkboxes. Each question expands on its own so the patient can open one and ignore the rest. The transcript is available behind a toggle for verification but is not the primary way to read. What is left is a preserved record.

Prototype

Switch between capture and review

The same conversation in both modes. Watch the checkboxes and inputs disappear and the record settle into something you read rather than operate.

9:41

Try it — switch modes to compare the two interfaces.

Same data, two interfaces. Nothing is duplicated; the affordances are simply withdrawn.

Independent expansion. Opening one question does not close another, so a patient can compare two answers side by side.

The transcript is optional. Some patients want the full text; others find it overwhelming. It is one tap away and never in the way.

The visual language

A reference sheet, deliberately not a component library.

The design system deliverable was a single sheet documenting foundations, atoms, molecules and screens, with each interaction state drawn separately. It is a reference, not a maintained library, and the distinction was the point: committing these patterns to the shared system before pilot validation would churn a resource other teams depend on.

Colour
primary.mainbackground.defaultbackground.papersurface.tintedtext.primarytext.secondaryerror.main
Type
Inter, weights 400 and 500 only. Display title 36/44 down to caption 12/16, with an 11/16 uppercase label at 0.5px tracking.
Spacing
4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32. Gutter 16, hero padding 24, section gap 32, answer indent 56.
Radius
4 inputs, 8 icon containers, 12 cards, 16 all 56pt primary buttons, 20 the upload pill, 28 sheet tops.
Elevation
None. Every component is flat; separation comes from tonal contrast and 1pt dividers, never shadow.
Widths
375pt to 440pt, safe areas 47 top and 34 bottom, 16pt gutters. Buttons 343 / 358 / 408.

The palette is a deep slate-teal on a warm off-white, with one tinted surface for the recording panel and one red reserved for destructive actions. Nothing is elevated — every component is flat, and separation comes from tonal contrast and one-point dividers. The closest the system comes to decoration is a rounded corner.

Prototype

Type a longer question and watch the row

The wrap-and-expand rule, live. Edit the question text and the row height is measured and reported as it changes. Short questions sit at 56pt; long ones grow to fit rather than clipping.

9:41

Try it — edit the question and watch the measured row height.

56pt is a minimum, not a height. Rows are specified with a minimum height so content can push them taller.

Three widths. 375pt, 390pt and 440pt. The same long question needs two lines on the smallest and one on the largest.

Touch targets hold. 44 × 44pt minimum tappable area throughout, with invisible padding where the visual element is smaller.

One inconsistency was found and closed during the audit: primary buttons in the auth flow used a 28px radius while action-bar buttons used 16px. All 56pt primary buttons are now 16px. The upload pill in the file picker keeps a 20px radius on purpose, because it is not a primary action and should not look like one.

How it was made

Two process diagrams from the board: design, then implementation.

This project ran with AI in the loop at two distinct points, and the board documents both. In the design phase, the model does dissection, drafting and specification writing; I keep judgment, cross-referencing and the final design. The checkpoint in the middle is a human one on purpose.

The implementation phase inverts the balance. Claude Code writes the code, reading design context through the Figma MCP server and generation rules from a CLAUDE.md file that translates the design system into instructions — token names instead of hex values, minimum heights instead of fixed ones, an explicit ban on truncating question text.

Claude Code does the implementation work. The designer remains the orchestrator, prompt author, and reviewer.AI-assisted implementation roadmap

Where it stands

Honestly: outputs, not outcomes.

There are no results to report. This phase produced five flow designs, one design system reference sheet and a working prototype, and it ended where it was scoped to end — at a stakeholder review that decides whether to invest further. Pilot user testing is the last node on the roadmap, not something that has happened.

Twenty open questions went into that review with the work, written down rather than resolved. The most consequential ones:

  • Is inline editing right, or would a dedicated screen give patients more room to think?
  • How prominent should the AI be? Is “Matched from recording” the right framing?
  • Should the system show its work — highlighting the transcript section each match came from?
  • What is the right confidence threshold for auto-matching versus leaving a question for the patient?
  • Should a patient be able to share a summary with a care partner or their primary care doctor?
  • Are the four suggested-question categories the right groupings, or should they follow cancer type or surveillance phase?

What happens next, as planned. Stakeholder feedback determines whether to invest in a fuller design system with components and tokens, a more committed prototype with complete interactive states, finalised engineering handoff documentation, and production specifications. The patterns documented in the reference sheet become proposal material for the monthly design system meeting, where they are reviewed and approved before anything is committed to the shared library.

What I'd do next

The part of this I would defend is the constraint work. Deciding early that Carry does not record, does not deliver results and does not let the AI author anything removed most of the hard questions before they became interface problems. The tone rules did the same thing for copy — a written ban on exclamation marks and celebration sounds trivial until you are writing the screen a patient sees after a fourth clear scan.

The part I would change is the order. This work is built on stated premises, and every one of them is testable. Before another design phase I would want to sit with people in surveillance and find out whether preparation is actually where the anxiety lives, whether they would record an appointment at all, and whether returning to an old conversation is a real behaviour or a designer's assumption about one. The prototype is a good instrument for that. It is not a substitute for it.

Sources for this page: the Carry ideation stories with acceptance criteria, the strategy board, and the design system audit. The four diagrams are reproductions of diagrams from that board — labels, terminology and relationships preserved, with changes limited to spacing, hierarchy and legibility.

The prototypes are HTML and CSS recreations of the Figma designs, running seeded data against simulated state machines. No backend, no real transcription, no patient data.
